title: ABS and Stability Control Overview
introduction:
Your brake pedal is not the only thing that can ask this Mustang to slow a wheel. I sort these systems by the problem they tackle: wheel lock during braking, wheelspin during acceleration, or a developing sideways slide. The shared brake hardware is a pit crew with several jobs.

This overview explains those jobs, the related driver aids and the pedal sensations that can accompany intervention. For equipped features, use the linked system descriptions and Owner’s Literature for operating instructions. This is a guide to understanding the systems, not a diagnostic, alignment or repair procedure.

edits.text: How ABS and Stability Control Help
edits.why: Introduces the functions and sensations covered by this overview.

edits.text: The anti-lock brake system (ABS) and stability control systems support the following features, each helping the driver maintain control in a different situation:
edits.why: Shared hardware can serve several purposes. Understanding the situation each feature addresses makes the names easier to distinguish.

edits.text: Anti-lock braking
Electronic brake force distribution (EBD)
Electronic Stability Control (ESC)
Hill start assist
Launch control
Line lock
Selectable drive mode
Supplemental braking assist
ABS support for adaptive cruise control
ABS support for collision avoidance
Traction control
During hard braking, anti-lock braking helps prevent the wheels from locking. Keeping the wheels turning helps the driver retain steering control.
edits.why: I associate ABS with braking grip: its intervention helps preserve the ability to steer while slowing.

edits.text: Electronic brake force distribution (EBD) helps maintain control by balancing braking between the front and rear wheels.
edits.why: The useful distinction here is front-to-rear braking balance, another job performed within this family of brake controls.

edits.text: Electronic Stability Control (ESC) helps prevent skids and sideways slides by regulating brake-fluid pressure at the brake calipers and reducing engine torque.
edits.why: Calipers turn hydraulic pressure into pad force against the brake discs. ESC can therefore influence the car’s motion through braking while also reducing the engine’s turning force.

edits.text: Hill start assist uses the ABS to hold the vehicle briefly on an incline. That short hold gives the driver time to move from the brake pedal to the accelerator without using the parking brake for the hill start.
edits.why: Think of this as a brief handover between pedals. The hold is temporary; this overview supplies no timed hold duration or activation sequence.

edits.text: Launch control coordinates the ABS and powertrain control module (PCM) to maximize traction during straight-line acceleration from a standstill. It uses a dedicated “drag start” traction-control calibration designed for high-grip surfaces.
edits.why: The calibration is tailored to getting moving from a standing start under those surface conditions. This description explains its purpose without supplying an engagement procedure.

edits.text: Line lock holds the front brakes applied while allowing the rear wheels to spin freely. This lets the rear tires be “conditioned” for maximum traction. Line lock is intended for race tracks only and must not be used on public roads.
edits.why: Holding the front brakes while freeing the rear wheels explains the feature’s name and its tire-conditioning role. The race-track restriction applies to its use.

edits.text: Selectable drive mode helps maintain traction by adapting the responses of the engine, transmission, electronic power assist steering (EPAS) and stability control system to the selected mode: normal, snow-wet, sport and track.
edits.why: A mode coordinates several responses across the car. EPAS supplies steering assistance through an electric motor, so steering assistance is part of that coordinated change.

edits.text: Supplemental braking assist uses the hydraulic pump motor and hydraulic control unit (HCU) to add braking assistance during severe vacuum loss at the brake booster or during a severe braking event.
edits.why: The booster normally helps reduce the driver’s braking effort. This feature explains how ABS hydraulic hardware can provide additional assistance under the stated conditions.

edits.text: The ABS supports adaptive cruise control by applying the brakes as needed to maintain the following gap selected by the driver. For the system’s operation and components, refer to [Cruise Control - System Operation and Component Description](#/document/G1693152) (419-03B Cruise Control - Vehicles With: Adaptive Cruise Control, Description and Operation).
edits.why: The cruise control module (CCM) uses radar to measure distance and relative speed, then requests braking from the ABS module and acceleration from the PCM. This ACC system does not function below 20 kmh (12 mph). During automatic deceleration, it discontinues braking at 20 kmh (12 mph): an audible alarm sounds, ABS automatic braking releases, and the driver must take over braking. Selecting standard cruise control removes lead-vehicle response and automatic braking; consult the Owner’s Literature for that selection and the indicator graphics. ABS can also request ACC deactivation when its estimated brake temperature is too high; an alarm sounds, and ACC remains deactivated until the estimated temperature returns to cooler operating conditions.

edits.text: The ABS supports collision avoidance by monitoring information and precharging the brake system, preparing it to help the vehicle stop in the shortest distance possible. For the system’s operation and components, refer to Collision Warning and Collision Avoidance System - System Operation and Component Description (419-03C Collision Warning and Collision Avoidance System, Description and Operation).
edits.why: Precharging prepares the brake system for a braking response. Continue to [Collision Warning and Collision Avoidance System - System Operation and Component Description](#/document/G1693169) for the separate system explanation; its full operating details are outside this overview.

edits.text: Traction control helps prevent loss of grip during acceleration by reducing drive-wheel spin.
edits.why: I associate traction control with putting engine power onto the road. This separates its acceleration role from ABS intervention during braking and ESC intervention during a developing skid.

edits.text: Some system noise and brake-pedal pulsation are normal during most ABS and stability control events. Immediately after either system activates, the brake pedal may also travel farther than usual.
edits.why: I pay attention to when the sensation occurs: during intervention or immediately afterward. That timing gives a pedal change or noise useful context when describing a concern; it does not establish the cause of symptoms occurring under other conditions.
